lesson.title: Evaluating models and assessing students
lesson.subtitle: Leakage, model cards and LLMs in coursework

video.title: Evaluating models and assessing students: Leakage, model cards and LLMs in coursework
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Prof Farah - head of department, Amman
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: Our best team topped the course leaderboard by a wide margin. Then we noticed they had tuned forty models on the test set. Their final score measured their persistence, not their model.
Today: how models are evaluated honestly, how to document them, and how to assess machine learning students when they can use language models.
Honest evaluation uses three splits. Train fits the weights, validation chooses the model and settings, and test is opened once, at the end. Every peek at test makes its score more optimistic.
With one percent positives, a model that always says no is ninety nine percent accurate and useless. Report precision, recall and calibration, and break results down by subgroup.
This classifier has ninety one percent recall overall. Split by group, it is ninety four percent for one and seventy two for the other. The average hid the gap.
Mitchell and colleagues proposed model cards: a short document with intended use, training data, metrics by subgroup, and known limits. Asking students to write one makes evaluation a habit.
Students can generate working code in seconds. So assess what a model cannot do for them. Use oral defences of their own notebooks, require an error analysis on their data, and grade the process.
Quick check! A team picked the best of forty models by validation score and reported that same score. Is it an honest estimate of performance on new data?
No. Picking the maximum of forty noisy scores selects luck as well as skill. Any score used to choose is optimistic, so report a fresh test score.

In the app, open the overfitting lab. Raise Freedom step by step and watch the error on new examples, which plays the validation set. Then ask students where they would stop, and why the test set must stay closed.
Your turn. Fraud is one transaction in a thousand. A model flags nothing and scores ninety nine point nine percent accuracy. Which metric exposes it?
Recall, which is zero. Remember: open the test set once, report metrics by subgroup, write a model card, and assess what language models cannot do for students.
Try it this term: add a ten minute oral defence to your next project. Ask each student to explain one error their model makes and one design choice they would change.

checkpoints.prompt: A team picked the best of 40 models by validation score and reported that score. Is it honest?

options.text: Yes, the model never trained on the validation set
No, choosing on it makes it optimistic; report a fresh test score
Yes, if the validation set is large

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: any score used to choose among many models is biased upwards; only data the choice never touched gives an honest estimate.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: choosing on the validation score makes it optimistic, so report a score on a fresh test set.

checkpoints.prompt: Fraud is 1 in 1,000. A model flags nothing and has 99.9% accuracy. Which metric exposes it?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: recall is 0, because it catches none of the fraud.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: recall, TP / (TP + FN), is 0 here, which accuracy hides.
